newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Russian buyer plans to double Ceylon tea imports.
newsitem.headline: Russian buyer plans to double Ceylon tea imports.

text.p: A top Russian importer of Sri Lankan tea to the world's biggest tea market said on Wednesday he planned to double purchases and expand into tourism in the Indian Ocean island.
"We're buying more and more pure Ceylon tea," Igor Lissinenko, president of the May Group of Companies, told Reuters. "We want to double the quantities we import in the next few years."

The company's Colombo-based subsidiary May Tea Export planned to buy up to 12 million kg of tea from Sri Lanka, the world's leading tea exporter, this year and raise purchases to 15 million kg next year, he said.
The company last year imported more than 11 million kg of Sri Lankan tea, he said.

"Until recently Western multinationals bought tea in bulk, blended it and sold it in the Russian market without identifying the origin. So the names of producer countries were kept out of the business," Lissinenko said.

"Our imports from Sri Lanka are sold as pure Ceylon tea. We do not blend with other origin teas. We spend a lot of money on promoting pure Ceylon tea," Lissinenko said. "We buy only packeted, value-added tea helping to create more opportunities for the Sri Lankan industry and more jobs."
Sri Lanka, whose tea exports are expected to hit a record 250 million kg this calendar year, meets about 20 percent of world demand.

Russia and other members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) bought 40 million kg of Sri Lankan tea last year, 17 percent of the island's total tea exports, and up 206 percent from a year earlier, brokers Forbes and Walker said.
Heavy buying by the CIS, which imports about 127 million kg of tea annually, sent Sri Lankan tea prices soaring to record highs in recent months.

"Russian consumers are very much concerned about quality," Lissinenko said. "In the near future we believe the standard of living of Russian consumers will grow and they'll be able to afford to buy quality products including the best quality tea."

However, prices for the island's main export crop peaked in mid-October, and brokers say they are concerned about Sri Lanka's heavy dependence on the markets of Russia and other former Soviet republics.
Lissinenko said his company's total annual imports of tea into the CIS were about 24 million kg, with India, China and Kenya accounting for the bulk of purchases from origins other than Sri Lanka.
Lissinenko said he held talks with tea industry officials and Prime Minister Sirima Bandaranaike and hoped to meet President Chandrika Kumaratunga during his visit to Colombo.

The May Group of Companies, which also imports coffee and other foodstuffs and is in the construction, transport and most recently the tourism business, hoped to expand into tourism in the island, he said.

"Our next step is to get into the local tourism business and encourage Russian tourists to visit Sri Lanka," he said. The island's tourism industry has been badly hit by the 13-year-long ethnic war against Tamil separatists.
